hook.support: Something isn't fair. The bus stop with no shelter. The skate park that closed. You could complain. Or you could **change** it.
hook.core: Something at your school, in your town or in your world isn't fair, isn't safe, or just doesn't make sense. The bus stop with no shelter. The skate park that got shut. The rule nobody can explain. You could complain about it. Or you could **change** it.

why.support: To change something, you have to **persuade** people. You need a clear **ask**, some evidence, and the right words for each audience.
why.core: Change rarely happens because one person is right. It happens because someone **persuades** the people with the power to act, and gets others to back them. That takes a clear **ask**, evidence, and the right text for each audience: a **petition** for decision-makers, a post for supporters, and a **speech** that makes people care.
why.extend: Advocacy is persuasion across audiences and modes. A campaign needs a precise, achievable ask directed at the right decision-maker, supported by evidence, and carried by texts adapted to each audience: a formal petition, a multimodal post and a spoken speech that position listeners to care and act.

articles.title: How to run a campaign

body.support:
Every big change started with someone speaking up.

**1. Choose a cause.** Something real and local, that can be changed.

**2. Make a clear ask.** Say what you want, and who can do it. *We ask the council to build a bus shelter.*

**3. Get evidence.** Count it. Take photos. Ask people.

**4. Write a petition.** Who it's to. The problem. Your evidence. Your ask. Space for names.

Anyone in Victoria, even under 18, can start a petition to Parliament.

**5. Make a post.** One picture, one message, what to do next. Under 16? Use school posters and noticeboards.

**6. Give a speech.** A story, the problem, a fact, your ask. Finish strong.

**7. Check what worked.** Did people sign? Did anyone reply?
body.core:
Every change that matters, from a bus shelter to the right to vote, started with someone deciding to speak up. Here's how a campaign works.

**1. Choose your cause.** Pick something real and local that you care about, and that can actually be changed: a bus stop with no shelter, a broken drinking tap, a skate park that closed.

**2. Make a clear ask.** *Things should be better* isn't an ask. A good **ask** says what you want, who can do it, and when: *We ask the council to build a shelter at the Main St bus stop before winter.* Then find the **decision-maker**: your principal, the student council, your local council, or a member of Parliament.

**3. Gather evidence.** Count it (*90 students use this stop every morning*). Photograph it. Ask people affected, and quote them (with permission). Find a fact from a reliable source.

**4. Write a petition.** A **petition** is a formal request signed by supporters. Keep it short:

- who it's to
- the problem, in one or two sentences
- your evidence
- your ask
- space for names (and nothing more private than people agree to).

Anyone in Victoria can start a petition to **State Parliament**, including people under 18. It must be made on the Parliament of Victoria website (not sites like Change.org), and a member of Parliament has to agree to sponsor it.

**5. Make a post for supporters.** One strong image, one clear message, and what to do: *Sign the petition at the office by Friday.* If you're under 16, use school channels, posters and noticeboards, not accounts on platforms like TikTok or Instagram.

**6. Give a speech.** A good one-minute speech has a hook (a story or a surprising fact), the problem, your evidence, the ask, and a strong last line. Speak slowly. Look up. Pause before the ask.

**7. Judge the impact.** Did people sign? Did the decision-maker reply? What would you do differently? Even if you don't win straight away, you've been heard, and you've learnt how change works.
body.extend:
Change happens when someone persuades the people with the power to act. A campaign is the set of texts that does it.

**1. Select a cause** that's specific, local and achievable.

**2. Frame the ask.** A strong **ask** names the change, the **decision-maker** responsible and a timeframe: *We ask Greenvale City Council to install a shelter at the Main St bus stop before June.* Choosing the right decision-maker (principal, student council, local council or a member of Parliament) decides where every text goes.

**3. Build the evidence base:** quantitative data you collect, images, testimony (with consent) and authoritative sources.

**4. Write the petition** as a short formal text: who it's to, the problem, the evidence, the ask, and a signature section that collects only what people agree to share. Any Victorian resident, including people under 18, can start an e-petition to State Parliament. It must be created on the Parliament of Victoria's website (third-party platforms aren't accepted), and a member must agree to sponsor it.

**5. Design a supporter post** in which image, message and call to action work together. Under-16s, now restricted from accounts on platforms such as TikTok and Instagram, can use school channels, posters and noticeboards.

**6. Deliver a speech** that moves from a hook (a story or a statistic) through the problem and evidence to the ask and a memorable close. Pace, pauses and eye contact do much of the persuading.

**7. Evaluate impact** against measurable signs (signatures, replies, decisions) and reflect on what you'd change. Many campaigns take years: the 1891 Victorian women's suffrage petition preceded the vote by 17 years.

caseStudies.title: The Monster Petition

body.support:
In **1891**, women in Victoria couldn't vote.

Women went door to door. In six weeks, they got nearly **30,000 signatures**. The petition was about **260 metres long**! People called it the **Monster Petition**.

It went to Parliament. But it didn't work straight away.

Women kept going. In **1908**, most Victorian women finally won the vote.

Campaigns can take a long time. Don't give up.
body.core:
In **1891**, women in Victoria couldn't vote. A group of women's organisations decided to prove that women wanted the vote, and that they weren't going to stop asking.

In about **six weeks**, volunteers went door to door across Victoria. They collected nearly **30,000 signatures**. When the pages were glued together onto fabric, the petition was about **260 metres long**. People called it the **Monster Petition**.

On **29 September 1891**, it was presented to the Parliament of Victoria.

Did it work straight away? **No.** The bill to give women the vote didn't pass. Women kept campaigning, and bill after bill failed.

Finally, in **1908**, seventeen years after the petition, most Victorian women won the right to vote.

The petition still exists. It's kept by the Parliament of Victoria. It shows two things about campaigns: **evidence of support** is powerful, and real change can take a long time. The people who started it didn't give up.
body.extend:
In **1891**, Victorian women couldn't vote. Women's organisations set out to show, not just say, that women wanted the vote.

Over about **six weeks**, volunteers went door to door and collected nearly **30,000 signatures**. Glued onto fabric, the petition stretched about **260 metres**. People called it the **Monster Petition**. It was presented to the Parliament of Victoria on **29 September 1891**.

It didn't work straight away. The bill that went with it failed, and so did many after it. Most Victorian women won the vote only in **1908**, seventeen years later.

The petition is still held by the Parliament of Victoria. It shows two things about campaigns. First, huge evidence of support turns an argument into proof of what the public wants. Second, change often takes years of campaigning and many texts, not one persuasive moment.

teacher.overview: The final Crossroads capstone, combining Digital Life and Your Voice. Students run a mini campaign for a real, achievable local cause: framing a precise ask for the right decision-maker, gathering evidence, writing a formal petition, designing a supporter post or poster, writing and delivering a one-minute persuasive speech, and evaluating impact. They learn that any Victorian resident, including people under 18, can start an e-petition to State Parliament through its website with a member's sponsorship. The case study is the 1891 Victorian Women's Suffrage (Monster) Petition.
prep: Agree with your principal which channels students can use (assembly, newsletter, noticeboards, student council) and which decision-makers they can approach.
Help students choose achievable causes. School-level causes are most likely to get a real reply.
Have the Parliament of Victoria's petition page ready to show.

steps: **Hook (10 min):** what would you change? List local, fixable things.
**Explicit teaching (10 min):** the ask, the decision-maker, evidence.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — The plan
steps: **Plan my campaign (20 min).** Conference: is the ask achievable, and is the decision-maker right?

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — The speech

steps: **Do it: launch the campaign (30 min),** or plan the launch.
**Judge the impact; Level Up, reflect (20 min):** quick check; request sign-off. (Revisit after the week of signatures.)

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** what you want, who can do it, when. Evidence: counts, photos, quotes (with consent), reliable facts. Petitions to the Parliament of Victoria: any resident, including under-18s; must be on the Parliament's website; a member must agree to sponsor it.

**Sort:** “school should be better” — weak; drinking taps by end of term — strong; stop climate change — weak (no decision-maker); reopen skate park on weekends — strong; ban homework — weak; trial a quiet space — strong.

**Petition:** 1 decision-maker; 2 problem; 3 evidence; 4 the ask; 5 who's asking; 6 privacy.

**Case study:** 30,000 signatures demonstrate widespread support rather than one person's view; they believed in the cause and kept building support; change can take years of campaigning (17 years here).

realityCheck: **Choose achievable causes.** Big global issues are worthy but hard to win. Guide students toward local asks with a real decision-maker, ideally at school level.
**Check with your principal first.** Campaigns about school issues need a respectful channel. Agree the rules before students launch.
**Privacy.** Petitions should collect names, suburbs and signatures only. No phone numbers or emails, and no photos of people without consent.
**Sensitive causes.** Some students will choose personal issues. Support them, and steer away from campaigns that target individuals.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It's the final capstone, and some campaigns genuinely change things. Celebrate the effort as well as the outcome.
